intro: At C2, the difference between good and excellent English is often one word: concerned or alarmed, annoyed or furious, slightly or dramatically. In this lesson you'll choose words with exactly the right strength, keep talking smoothly when a word suddenly disappears, and turn a point up or down with the right partner word. Warm-up: think of the last time a word was on the tip of your tongue in English. What did you do?
teachingNotes: This speaking lesson builds on c1-debate (buying time, clarifying, concede and counter), c1-connotation (synonyms with different feelings: slim / skinny), c1-hedging (arguably, to some extent, the certainty scale) and c1-modal-nuance (be bound to / be likely to). From b2-collocations the learner knows highly likely, deeply concerned, bitterly disappointed, fully aware and strongly agree (not strongly unlikely); from c1-world-englishes What I mean is … / Let me put it another way; from c1-listening-implicit that or rather / I mean mark the final, correct version. Recap in a line, don't re-teach. New here: DEGREE (near-synonym scales), talking around a missing word with repair phrases, and non-gradable adjectives with absolutely / utterly, downtoners, by no means and far from.

Fine nuance (fine-nuance). Scales, weakest to strongest: concerned (khawatir/prihatin, calm, formal) < worried < alarmed (sudden fear that something dangerous may happen) < panicked (so frightened you can't think clearly); annoyed (kesal) < irritated (jengkel; close to annoyed, often about something repeated) < furious (marah besar); pleased (formal: We are pleased to announce) < delighted < thrilled (very pleased and excited); likely < highly likely < bound to (almost certain); slightly < somewhat (agak, a bit formal, often before an adjective or comparative: somewhat higher) < considerably < dramatically (drastis). Same family, different job: criticise (say what's wrong, can be mild; American criticize) vs condemn (say publicly that something is morally wrong: violence, corruption); claim (others may doubt it) vs assert (firmly, confidently) vs allege (accuse without proof yet; alleged / allegedly in the news); reluctant to (enggan, may still do it) vs unwilling to (stronger, usually won't) vs refuse to (clearly says no; a verb, so no 'was'). Indonesian traps: sangat + one word for every level; casual 'aku panik' carried into a report as 'the team panicked'; menolak = refuse to do something, but a proposal is usually rejected or turned down. The middle of a scale overlaps (annoyed / irritated, concerned / worried): only test the clearly different ends, with context that states the degree.

Reformulating (reformulate-smoothly). The node's common error: going silent or switching to Indonesian (apa ya namanya… itu lho…) when a word is missing. Silence hands the turn to someone else, and Indonesian loses international listeners. Teach four paraphrase strategies: describe the function (It's the thing you use to … / the person who … / the place where …), give an example (like when …), use a more general word, the 'kata payung' (a kind of tool / a type of permit), use the opposite (the opposite of generous, not deep). Repair phrases and what each does: What I mean is … (clarify), Let me put it another way (start a new explanation), Or rather … (swap in a more accurate word), In other words … (say it more simply), To be more precise … (add the exact detail or number), I'm looking for the word … / What's it called? (then describe), It's on the tip of my tongue (the same image as 'di ujung lidah'). Keeping the floor: Well, let me think … / How shall I put it … / Hang on, what's the word … One short filler is natural; a string of them is not.

Emphasising and softening (emphasise-soften). Gradable adjectives (tired, important, cold) take a bit / quite / very / extremely. Non-gradable ones already mean the maximum (exhausted, essential, vital, freezing, furious, delighted, perfect, impossible, ridiculous) and take absolutely / utterly / completely / totally (really also works), not very: absolutely essential, not very essential; slightly perfect makes no sense. utterly is mostly used with negative or unwelcome ideas (utterly exhausted, utterly unacceptable); absolutely works with both. Downtoners: a little / a bit (informal), slightly, somewhat (more formal). rather: in British English rather + a negative word softly criticises (rather expensive), but with a positive word it can mean 'very', a pleasant surprise (That was rather good!). quite good = fairly good in British English but very good in American English; quite + non-gradable = completely (quite right). Stance: arguably (an opinion you can defend), to some extent (partly), by no means (a strong not: by no means certain), far from + adjective / noun (far from perfect, far from easy: polite in form, strong in meaning). Indonesian traps: sangat penting sekali (double intensifier) → one is enough; jauh dari kata sempurna → far from perfect, not 'far from the word perfect'.

C2 honesty: much of this is style, and near-synonyms overlap. Accept any natural alternative (worried / concerned in casual speech, somewhat / slightly, absolutely / utterly / totally with a non-gradable word, tool / thing / device in a description) and only mark clear faults: the wrong end of a scale for the stated situation, very or slightly with a non-gradable word, a phrase that does the wrong job (In other words for a correction), silence or Indonesian instead of a paraphrase, 'far from the word perfect'. When the learner practises, give them a word they 'can't remember' (shredder, receipt, auditor, stingy) and let them talk around it, then react to the content before correcting ONE thing.

Limits: every structure is available at C2; the point is precise choice, not new grammar. Don't teach rare literary intensifiers (supremely, eminently) or long lists of synonyms; if the learner uses one correctly, accept it and say it's less common. Contexts: meetings with international partners, video calls with Melbourne or Singapore, ministries and NGOs in Jakarta, campuses in Yogyakarta and Bandung, offices in Surabaya, news reports; keep facts general and don't invent statistics about real organisations.

keyPoints.title: Choose the word with the right strength
keyPoints.explanation: Many near-synonyms sit on a scale: concerned < worried < alarmed < panicked; annoyed < irritated < furious; pleased < delighted < thrilled; likely < highly likely < bound to; slightly < somewhat < considerably < dramatically. Others differ in what they do: criticise (say what's wrong) vs condemn (say it's morally wrong); claim vs assert (firmly) vs allege (accuse without proof yet); reluctant to (may still do it) vs refuse to (says no). Indonesian adds sangat; English usually picks a different word.

examples.en: The board is concerned about the delay, but there's no need to change the plan.
examples.id: Direksi khawatir soal keterlambatan itu, tapi rencananya tidak perlu diubah.

examples.en: Human rights groups condemned the attack on journalists.
examples.id: Kelompok-kelompok HAM mengecam serangan terhadap para wartawan.

examples.en: Exports rose considerably, from Rp 2 trillion to Rp 2.6 trillion.
examples.id: Ekspor naik cukup besar, dari Rp 2 triliun menjadi Rp 2,6 triliun.

id.title: Pilih kata dengan kekuatan yang pas
id.explanation: Banyak kata yang mirip artinya berada pada satu skala: concerned < worried < alarmed < panicked; annoyed < irritated < furious; pleased < delighted < thrilled; likely < highly likely < bound to; slightly < somewhat < considerably < dramatically. Ada juga yang berbeda fungsinya: criticise (mengatakan apa yang salah) vs condemn (mengecam karena salah secara moral); claim vs assert (dengan tegas) vs allege (menuduh tanpa bukti dulu); reluctant to (enggan, mungkin tetap melakukannya) vs refuse to (menolak). Bahasa Indonesia menambahkan sangat; bahasa Inggris biasanya memilih kata yang berbeda.

keyPoints.title: Keep going when a word disappears
keyPoints.explanation: Don't go silent and don't switch to Indonesian. Talk around the gap: describe what it does (It's the thing you use to … / the person who …), give an example (like when …), use a more general word (a kind of tool) or the opposite (the opposite of polite). Repair phrases tell the listener what you're doing: What I mean is …, Let me put it another way, Or rather … (a more accurate word), In other words … (more simply), To be more precise … (the exact detail), I'm looking for the word …. Keep the floor with Well, let me think … / How shall I put it ….

examples.en: I'm looking for the word … it's the person who checks a company's accounts every year.
examples.id: Saya lagi mencari katanya … orang yang memeriksa keuangan perusahaan setiap tahun.

examples.en: It was a mistake, or rather a misunderstanding between the two teams.
examples.id: Itu sebuah kesalahan, atau lebih tepatnya salah paham antara dua tim.

examples.en: Sales were good. To be more precise, they were 12% above target.
examples.id: Penjualannya bagus. Tepatnya, 12% di atas target.

id.title: Terus bicara saat kata tiba-tiba hilang
id.explanation: Jangan diam dan jangan pindah ke bahasa Indonesia. Jelaskan dengan cara lain: sebutkan fungsinya (It's the thing you use to … / the person who …), beri contoh (like when …), pakai kata yang lebih umum (a kind of tool) atau kebalikannya (the opposite of polite). Frasa perbaikan memberi tahu pendengar apa yang sedang kamu lakukan: What I mean is …, Let me put it another way, Or rather … (kata yang lebih tepat), In other words … (lebih sederhana), To be more precise … (detail yang persis), I'm looking for the word …. Pertahankan giliran bicaramu dengan Well, let me think … / How shall I put it ….

keyPoints.title: Turn a point up or down precisely
keyPoints.explanation: Words that already mean the maximum (essential, exhausted, freezing, furious, perfect, impossible) take absolutely / utterly / completely, not very: absolutely essential, utterly exhausted. utterly is mostly for negative ideas. To soften: slightly, somewhat, a little (British rather can soften or, with a positive word, intensify). For your stance: arguably (an opinion you can defend), to some extent (partly), by no means (definitely not), far from + adjective (far from perfect).

examples.en: After the night shift, the nurses were utterly exhausted.
examples.id: Setelah sif malam, para perawat benar-benar kelelahan.

examples.en: Success is by no means guaranteed.
The new system is far from perfect, but it's faster than the old one.
examples.id: Sistem baru itu jauh dari sempurna, tapi lebih cepat daripada yang lama.

id.title: Naikkan atau turunkan kekuatan poinmu dengan presisi
id.explanation: Kata yang sudah bermakna maksimal (essential, exhausted, freezing, furious, perfect, impossible) dipasangkan dengan absolutely / utterly / completely, bukan very: absolutely essential, utterly exhausted. utterly biasanya untuk hal negatif. Untuk melunakkan: slightly, somewhat, a little (rather dalam bahasa Inggris Britania bisa melunakkan atau, dengan kata positif, justru menguatkan). Untuk sikapmu: arguably (pendapat yang bisa kamu pertahankan), to some extent (sebagian), by no means (sama sekali tidak), far from + kata sifat (far from perfect).

guidedPractice.prompt: A client in Surabaya shouted on the phone and threatened to cancel the whole contract. 'Angry' sounds too weak. Complete with one word (= marah besar): The client was ___.
guidedPractice.hint: The anger scale: annoyed (kesal) → irritated (jengkel) → furious (marah besar). Shouting and threatening is the top of the scale.

guidedPractice.prompt: After violence at a student protest, the university released a strong public statement saying the violence was morally wrong. Complete with one word: The rector ___ the violence.
guidedPractice.hint: criticise = say what's wrong (can be mild); condemn = mengecam: say publicly that something is morally wrong.

guidedPractice.prompt: On a video call, you can't remember the word 'umbrella'. Use a more general word. Complete with one word: It's a ___ of thing you hold over your head when it rains.
guidedPractice.hint: a kind of … / a sort of … = semacam …: name the bigger group, then describe.

guidedPractice.prompt: The sunrise from Mount Bromo was the most beautiful thing you've ever seen. Complete with one word (not very): The view was ___ amazing.
guidedPractice.hint: amazing already means 'extremely good', so it takes absolutely (or really), not very.

independentPractice.prompt: In a meeting, Rina said 'The report is ready' and wants to add the exact detail. Complete with one word: To be more ___, the first draft is ready and the charts are coming tomorrow.
independentPractice.hint: To be more precise = tepatnya: it adds the exact detail.

independentPractice.prompt: You think gudeg is perhaps the best dish in Yogyakarta: an opinion, but one you can defend. Complete with one word: Gudeg is ___ the best dish in Yogyakarta.
independentPractice.hint: arguably = bisa dibilang: it marks an opinion you can defend, often before a superlative (the best).

independentPractice.prompt: Budi has been late to every Monday meeting this year. Complete with one word (= hampir pasti): He's ___ to be late again next Monday.
independentPractice.hint: likely < highly likely < bound to: bound to = almost certain, often from experience.

assessment.prompt: Bu Ani is writing a calm, formal statement for the city health office in Surabaya about a small rise in dengue cases. She doesn't want to frighten anyone. Choose the best word from this list: concerned, alarmed, panicked. 'We are ___ about the rise in dengue cases and are monitoring the situation closely.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: concerned (khawatir/prihatin, but calm and formal: the usual word in official statements). 'worried' = 70 (the right degree, but less formal and not in the list). 'alarmed' = 20 (too strong: it suggests sudden fear and would frighten people). 'panicked' = 0 (lost control: the opposite of a calm statement).

assessment.prompt: A Jakarta newspaper reports that a company director may have paid a bribe to win a government contract. The police are investigating, and nothing has been proven in court. Choose the best word from this list: alleged, asserted, criticised. 'The director denies any involvement in the ___ bribe.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: alleged (= diduga: someone says it happened, but there's no proof yet; journalists use it so they don't accuse anyone before a court decides). 'claimed' = 30 (understandable, but 'the alleged bribe' is the standard phrase). 'asserted' = 0 (it means stated firmly; it doesn't describe a bribe). 'criticised' = 0.

assessment.prompt: In a job interview in Jakarta, Dimas explains his last project, but the interviewer looks confused. Dimas wants to start again and explain it in a completely different way. Complete with one word: Let me put it another ___.
assessment.rubric: Correct: way (Let me put it another way = coba saya jelaskan dengan cara lain: a new explanation, not just the same words again). 'manner' = 40 (understandable but not the phrase). 'word' or 'words' = 20 (confused with In other words). Silence or an answer in Indonesian = 0.

assessment.prompt: In a project meeting in Bandung, Sari says the work will take three weeks, then immediately corrects herself to a more accurate estimate. Complete with one word: It'll take three weeks, or ___ closer to four.
assessment.rubric: Correct: rather (or rather = atau lebih tepatnya: it swaps what you just said for a more accurate version, and the listener knows the second version is the real one). 'actually' = 60 (natural in speech, but 'or rather' is the repair phrase). 'maybe' = 30 (sounds unsure instead of correcting). 'in other words' = 0 (that says the same thing again, it doesn't correct it).

assessment.prompt: On a video call with a partner in Melbourne, Budi forgets the word 'stapler'. Instead of stopping, he describes what it does. Complete with one word: It's the ___ you use to join sheets of paper together with a small piece of metal.
assessment.rubric: Correct: thing (It's the thing you use to … = benda yang dipakai untuk …: describing the function). tool, machine, device, gadget, item or object are also correct. 'stapler' = 20 (that's the missing word, and 'the stapler you use to …' doesn't work as a description). An Indonesian word (e.g. 'stepler', 'staples') = 0.

assessment.prompt: At a café in Bandung, a coffee now costs Rp 2,000 more than last month, and customers haven't complained. The owner wants to make the change sound small, but honest. Complete with one word: The new prices are ___ higher than last month's.
assessment.rubric: Correct: slightly (= sedikit). somewhat, marginally, a little, a bit and a tad are also correct. 'rather' = 60 (it can soften, but in British English 'rather higher' often suggests more than expected). 'considerably', 'much', 'far' or 'dramatically' = 0 (they make the change sound big). 'very' = 0 (very doesn't go with a comparative like higher).

assessment.prompt: Your team has moved to a new office in Yogyakarta. It has no windows, the lift is broken and the Wi-Fi keeps dropping. In an email to your manager, you want to say politely but clearly that it is not good at all. Complete with one word: The new office is ___ from ideal.
assessment.rubric: Correct: far (far from ideal = jauh dari ideal: polite in form but strong in meaning, i.e. quite bad). 'a long way' = 70 (a long way from ideal is natural, but it's three words). 'very' or 'not' = 0 (very from / not from don't work). 'away' = 10.

material.title: Same idea, different strength: near-synonym scales

blocks.text:
Quick recap: from the connotation lesson you know that near-synonyms can carry different **feelings** (*slim / skinny*). From hedging and modal nuance you have a certainty scale (*probably → almost certainly*) and *bound to*. At C2 the next step is **degree** (*tingkat kekuatan*): words for the same kind of thing at a different strength. The right one makes you sound precise instead of dramatic, or too weak.

Indonesian often uses one word plus **sangat** (*sangat khawatir, sangat marah, sangat senang*). English usually has a **separate word** for each level:
- **Worry:** *concerned* (khawatir, prihatin, but calm; formal) → *worried* (khawatir) → *alarmed* (cemas dan kaget: something dangerous may happen) → *panicked* (panik: so frightened you can't think clearly).
- **Anger:** *annoyed* (kesal) → *irritated* (jengkel; close to annoyed, often about something that keeps happening) → *furious* (marah besar).
- **Happiness:** *pleased* (senang; polite and formal: *We are pleased to announce …*) → *delighted* (sangat senang) → *thrilled* (senang sekali dan bersemangat).
- **Probability:** *likely* (kemungkinan besar) → *highly likely* (sangat mungkin) → *bound to* (pasti: almost certain).
- **Change:** *slightly* (sedikit) → *somewhat* (agak; a bit formal, often before an adjective: *somewhat higher*) → *considerably* (cukup besar) → *dramatically* (drastis).

The scale is a guide, not a ruler: *annoyed* and *irritated* overlap, and so do *concerned* and *worried*. But the **ends** of a scale are clearly different: a 2% rise didn't rise *dramatically*, and a manager who is *concerned* hasn't *panicked*.

id.text:
Ulasan singkat: dari pelajaran konotasi kamu tahu bahwa kata yang mirip artinya bisa membawa **rasa** yang berbeda (*slim / skinny*). Dari hedging dan modal nuance kamu punya skala kepastian (*probably → almost certainly*) dan *bound to*. Di C2 langkah berikutnya adalah **degree** (*tingkat kekuatan*): kata untuk hal yang sama tapi dengan kekuatan berbeda. Kata yang tepat membuatmu terdengar presisi, bukan dramatis atau terlalu lemah.

Bahasa Indonesia sering memakai satu kata plus **sangat** (*sangat khawatir, sangat marah, sangat senang*). Bahasa Inggris biasanya punya **kata tersendiri** untuk setiap tingkat:
- **Khawatir:** *concerned* (khawatir, prihatin, tapi tenang; formal) → *worried* (khawatir) → *alarmed* (cemas dan kaget: ada sesuatu yang berbahaya) → *panicked* (panik: begitu takut sampai tidak bisa berpikir jernih).
- **Marah:** *annoyed* (kesal) → *irritated* (jengkel; mirip annoyed, sering karena hal yang terus terulang) → *furious* (marah besar).
- **Senang:** *pleased* (senang; sopan dan formal: *We are pleased to announce …*) → *delighted* (sangat senang) → *thrilled* (senang sekali dan bersemangat).
- **Kemungkinan:** *likely* (kemungkinan besar) → *highly likely* (sangat mungkin) → *bound to* (pasti: hampir pasti terjadi).
- **Perubahan:** *slightly* (sedikit) → *somewhat* (agak; agak formal, sering sebelum kata sifat: *somewhat higher*) → *considerably* (cukup besar) → *dramatically* (drastis).

Skala ini panduan, bukan penggaris: *annoyed* dan *irritated* tumpang tindih, begitu juga *concerned* dan *worried*. Tapi **ujung-ujung** skalanya jelas berbeda: kenaikan 2% tidak naik *dramatically*, dan manajer yang *concerned* belum *panicked*.

rows.en: The board is concerned about the delay, but there's no need to change the plan.
rows.id: Direksi khawatir soal keterlambatan itu, tapi rencananya tidak perlu diubah.

rows.en: Residents were alarmed when the river rose two metres in one night.
rows.id: Warga cemas dan kaget ketika sungai naik dua meter dalam semalam.

rows.en: I was a bit annoyed that the meeting started late.
rows.id: Saya agak kesal karena rapatnya mulai terlambat.

rows.en: Pak Hasan was furious when he found out the report had been leaked.
rows.id: Pak Hasan marah besar ketika tahu laporan itu bocor.
rows.note: the top of the anger scale

rows.en: We are delighted to welcome Dr. Wulan to the team.
rows.id: Kami sangat senang menyambut Dr. Wulan di tim kami.

rows.en: Exports rose considerably, from Rp 2 trillion to Rp 2.6 trillion.
rows.id: Ekspor naik cukup besar, dari Rp 2 triliun menjadi Rp 2,6 triliun.

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap: panik.** In Indonesian, *aku panik* is often casual (*HP-ku ketinggalan, panik!*). English *panicked* has a casual use too (*I panicked when I couldn't find my phone*), but in a meeting or a report, *the team panicked* means people lost control: a serious thing to say about colleagues. If you mean khawatir, say *worried* or, more formally, *concerned*. The same goes for **sangat**: *very angry* is fine, but *furious* says it in one precise word.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: panik.** Dalam bahasa Indonesia, *aku panik* sering dipakai santai (*HP-ku ketinggalan, panik!*). *panicked* dalam bahasa Inggris juga punya pemakaian santai (*I panicked when I couldn't find my phone*), tapi dalam rapat atau laporan, *the team panicked* berarti orang-orang kehilangan kendali: pernyataan yang serius tentang rekan kerja. Kalau maksudmu khawatir, katakan *worried* atau, lebih formal, *concerned*. Begitu juga dengan **sangat**: *very angry* tidak salah, tapi *furious* mengatakannya dalam satu kata yang presisi.

blocks.prompt: Bu Ani's flight from Jakarta to Bali left fifteen minutes late. It was a small problem and she was only mildly bothered. Complete: She was a little ___.
blocks.explain: **annoyed** (kesal) is the mild end of the anger scale, and *a little* fits it. *furious* is the top of the scale, far too strong for fifteen minutes (and *a little furious* contradicts itself). *alarmed* means afraid that something dangerous may happen, which a short delay isn't.

id.prompt: Penerbangan Bu Ani dari Jakarta ke Bali berangkat lima belas menit terlambat. Masalahnya kecil dan dia hanya sedikit terganggu. Lengkapi: She was a little ___.
id.explain: **annoyed** (kesal) adalah ujung ringan dari skala marah, dan *a little* cocok dengannya. *furious* adalah puncak skala, terlalu kuat untuk lima belas menit (dan *a little furious* bertentangan dengan dirinya sendiri). *alarmed* berarti takut ada sesuatu yang berbahaya, padahal keterlambatan singkat tidak berbahaya.

id.title: Ide sama, kekuatan berbeda: skala kata yang mirip

material.title: Same family, different job: condemn, allege, reluctant

blocks.text:
Some near-synonyms differ not only in strength but in **what exactly they do**. You'll meet these in the news and in formal meetings:
- **criticise** (mengkritik) = say what's wrong with something; it can be mild or helpful. **condemn** (mengecam, mengutuk) = say publicly and strongly that something is **morally wrong**: violence, corruption, discrimination. *The auditors criticised the timetable* (it has problems); *The ministry condemned the attack* (it is wrong). *criticise* is the British spelling; American English writes *criticize*.
- **claim** (mengklaim) = say something is true, while others may doubt it. **assert** (menegaskan) = state firmly and confidently. **allege** (menuduh) = say that someone did something wrong or illegal, **without proof yet**. In the news: *the **alleged** bribe* (suap yang diduga), *He **allegedly** paid …* (diduga membayar …). Journalists use it so they don't accuse anyone before a court decides.
- **reluctant to** (enggan, berat hati) = you don't want to, but you may still do it. **unwilling to** (tidak mau) = stronger: you usually won't. **refuse to** (menolak) = you clearly say no. Grammar: *reluctant* and *unwilling* are adjectives (*She **was** reluctant to sign*), but *refuse* is a verb (*She refused to sign*, not *She was refused to sign*).

id.text:
Beberapa kata yang mirip berbeda bukan hanya dalam kekuatan, tapi juga dalam **apa persisnya fungsinya**. Kamu akan menemukannya di berita dan rapat formal:
- **criticise** (mengkritik) = mengatakan apa yang salah dari sesuatu; bisa ringan atau membangun. **condemn** (mengecam, mengutuk) = mengatakan secara terbuka dan keras bahwa sesuatu **salah secara moral**: kekerasan, korupsi, diskriminasi. *The auditors criticised the timetable* (jadwalnya bermasalah); *The ministry condemned the attack* (serangannya salah). *criticise* adalah ejaan Britania; bahasa Inggris Amerika menulis *criticize*.
- **claim** (mengklaim) = mengatakan sesuatu benar, padahal orang lain mungkin meragukannya. **assert** (menegaskan) = menyatakan dengan tegas dan yakin. **allege** (menuduh) = mengatakan seseorang melakukan sesuatu yang salah atau melanggar hukum, **tanpa bukti dulu**. Di berita: *the **alleged** bribe* (suap yang diduga), *He **allegedly** paid …* (diduga membayar …). Wartawan memakainya supaya tidak menuduh siapa pun sebelum pengadilan memutuskan.
- **reluctant to** (enggan, berat hati) = kamu tidak ingin, tapi mungkin tetap melakukannya. **unwilling to** (tidak mau) = lebih kuat: biasanya kamu tidak akan melakukannya. **refuse to** (menolak) = kamu jelas berkata tidak. Tata bahasanya: *reluctant* dan *unwilling* adalah kata sifat (*She **was** reluctant to sign*), tapi *refuse* adalah kata kerja (*She refused to sign*, bukan *She was refused to sign*).

rows.en: The auditors criticised the way the budget was managed.
rows.id: Para auditor mengkritik cara anggaran itu dikelola.

rows.en: Human rights groups condemned the attack on journalists.
rows.id: Kelompok-kelompok HAM mengecam serangan terhadap para wartawan.

id.note: salah secara moral, diucapkan secara terbuka

rows.en: The company claims its app is the fastest in Indonesia.
rows.id: Perusahaan itu mengklaim aplikasinya yang tercepat di Indonesia.

rows.en: Police allege that two staff members sold customer data.
rows.id: Polisi menuduh dua karyawan menjual data pelanggan.

rows.en: Budi was reluctant to move to Surabaya, but he agreed in the end.
rows.id: Budi enggan pindah ke Surabaya, tapi akhirnya dia setuju.

rows.en: The landlord refused to return the deposit.
rows.id: Pemilik kos menolak mengembalikan uang jaminan.

blocks.text: Indonesian trap: **menolak** covers two English verbs. For an action, use **refuse to**: *He refused to sign the contract.* For a proposal, an application or an offer, English usually says **reject** or **turn down**: *The committee rejected our proposal. She turned down the job in Bali.* (*refuse an offer* is also possible.) And don't copy *dia menolak untuk* as *he was refused to*: that means someone else said no to him.

id.text: Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: **menolak** mencakup dua kata kerja bahasa Inggris. Untuk tindakan, pakai **refuse to**: *He refused to sign the contract.* Untuk proposal, lamaran atau tawaran, bahasa Inggris biasanya memakai **reject** atau **turn down**: *The committee rejected our proposal. She turned down the job in Bali.* (*refuse an offer* juga bisa.) Dan jangan menyalin *dia menolak untuk* menjadi *he was refused to*: itu berarti orang lain yang menolak dia.

blocks.prompt: After a violent attack on a group of students, the university released a strong public statement saying the attack was morally wrong. Which sentence is precise?
options: The university was reluctant to criticise the attack.
blocks.explain: **condemn** = say publicly and strongly that something is morally wrong, exactly what a strong statement about violence does. *claimed the attack* would mean the university said it carried out the attack. *reluctant to criticise* says the opposite of a strong statement.

id.prompt: Setelah serangan kekerasan terhadap sekelompok mahasiswa, universitas mengeluarkan pernyataan publik yang keras bahwa serangan itu salah secara moral. Kalimat mana yang presisi?
id.explain: **condemn** = mengatakan secara terbuka dan keras bahwa sesuatu salah secara moral, persis yang dilakukan pernyataan keras tentang kekerasan. *claimed the attack* berarti universitas mengaku melakukan serangan itu. *reluctant to criticise* justru kebalikan dari pernyataan yang keras.

id.title: Satu keluarga, fungsi berbeda: condemn, allege, reluctant

material.title: When the word won't come: paraphrase and repair

blocks.text:
Everyone loses words, native speakers included. What makes C2 speakers sound fluent is that **they don't stop**: they talk around the gap so smoothly that the listener hardly notices. You've met some tools already: *What I mean is …* for a listener who looks lost (World Englishes), and *or rather* as a signal that the last version is the real one (implicit listening). Now use them for your own gaps.

**Four ways to talk around a missing word** (this is *paraphrasing*: menjelaskan dengan kata lain):
- **Describe what it does:** *It's the thing you use to … / the person who … / the place where …* (*the person who checks a company's accounts* = an auditor)
- **Give an example:** *like when … / for example, …* (*It's like when the bank blocks your card to protect you*)
- **Use a more general word**, a *kata payung* (the bigger group it belongs to): *It's a kind of tool / a type of document / some sort of permit*
- **Use the opposite:** *the opposite of polite* (= rude), *not deep* (= shallow)

**Repair phrases** tell the listener exactly what you're doing:
- **What I mean is …** (maksud saya …): clarify what you meant.
- **Let me put it another way.** (coba saya jelaskan dengan cara lain): start again with a different explanation.
- **Or rather …** (atau lebih tepatnya …): swap a word for a more accurate one: *a mistake, or rather a misunderstanding*.
- **In other words, …** (dengan kata lain …): say the same point more simply.
- **To be more precise, …** (tepatnya …): add the exact detail or number.
- **I'm looking for the word …** / **What's it called?** (apa ya namanya?): then describe it. *It's on the tip of my tongue* = sudah di ujung lidah: the same picture as in Indonesian!

**Keep the floor** (tetap memegang giliran bicara): *Well, let me think … / How shall I put it … / Hang on, what's the word …* These short fillers tell people you haven't finished, so nobody jumps in. One is natural; five in a row are not.

id.text:
Semua orang pernah lupa kata, termasuk penutur asli. Yang membuat pembicara C2 terdengar lancar adalah **mereka tidak berhenti**: mereka menjelaskan di sekitar celah itu dengan begitu mulus sehingga pendengar hampir tidak sadar. Kamu sudah kenal beberapa alatnya: *What I mean is …* untuk pendengar yang tampak bingung (World Englishes), dan *or rather* sebagai tanda bahwa versi terakhir adalah yang sebenarnya (listening implisit). Sekarang pakai untuk celahmu sendiri.

**Empat cara menjelaskan kata yang hilang** (ini disebut *paraphrasing*: menjelaskan dengan kata lain):
- **Jelaskan fungsinya:** *It's the thing you use to … / the person who … / the place where …* (*the person who checks a company's accounts* = auditor)
- **Beri contoh:** *like when … / for example, …* (*It's like when the bank blocks your card to protect you*)
- **Pakai kata yang lebih umum**, sebuah *kata payung* (kelompok yang lebih besar): *It's a kind of tool / a type of document / some sort of permit*
- **Pakai kebalikannya:** *the opposite of polite* (= rude), *not deep* (= shallow)

**Frasa perbaikan** memberi tahu pendengar apa yang sedang kamu lakukan:
- **What I mean is …** (maksud saya …): memperjelas maksudmu.
- **Let me put it another way.** (coba saya jelaskan dengan cara lain): mulai lagi dengan penjelasan yang berbeda.
- **Or rather …** (atau lebih tepatnya …): mengganti kata dengan yang lebih akurat: *a mistake, or rather a misunderstanding*.
- **In other words, …** (dengan kata lain …): mengatakan poin yang sama dengan lebih sederhana.
- **To be more precise, …** (tepatnya …): menambahkan detail atau angka yang persis.
- **I'm looking for the word …** / **What's it called?** (apa ya namanya?): lalu jelaskan. *It's on the tip of my tongue* = sudah di ujung lidah: gambarannya sama dengan bahasa Indonesia!

**Pertahankan giliran bicara**: *Well, let me think … / How shall I put it … / Hang on, what's the word …* Pengisi singkat ini memberi tahu orang bahwa kamu belum selesai, jadi tidak ada yang menyela. Satu itu wajar; lima berturut-turut tidak.

rows.en: It's a kind of permit you need before you build a house.
rows.id: Itu semacam izin yang kamu perlukan sebelum membangun rumah.

rows.en: It's like when the bank blocks your card to protect you.
rows.id: Itu seperti saat bank memblokir kartumu untuk melindungimu.

rows.en: What I mean is that the deadline is too tight, not that the idea is bad.
rows.id: Maksud saya, tenggatnya terlalu mepet, bukan idenya yang jelek.

rows.en: The venue costs more than our whole budget. In other words, we can't afford it.
rows.id: Biaya tempatnya lebih besar daripada seluruh anggaran kita. Dengan kata lain, kita tidak sanggup membayarnya.

blocks.text: **The common mistake: going silent or switching to Indonesian.** In a meeting with international partners, a long silence hands your turn to someone else, and *apa ya namanya … itu lho …* loses everyone who doesn't speak Indonesian (and breaks the flow even for those who do). Translate the habit instead: *apa namanya* → **What's it called?**, *itu lho* → **you know, the …**, and then **describe**. A clear description beats a perfect word that never comes: *We need the … what's it called … the paper that shows you've paid* works fine even if *receipt* never arrives.

id.text: **Kesalahan umum: diam atau pindah ke bahasa Indonesia.** Dalam rapat dengan mitra internasional, diam terlalu lama menyerahkan giliranmu ke orang lain, dan *apa ya namanya … itu lho …* membuat semua orang yang tidak bisa bahasa Indonesia kehilangan jejak (dan memutus alur bahkan bagi yang bisa). Terjemahkan kebiasaannya: *apa namanya* → **What's it called?**, *itu lho* → **you know, the …**, lalu **jelaskan**. Penjelasan yang jelas lebih baik daripada kata sempurna yang tidak kunjung muncul: *We need the … what's it called … the paper that shows you've paid* tetap berhasil walaupun kata *receipt* tidak pernah teringat.

blocks.prompt: Dr. Wulan presents a survey in Yogyakarta. She says 'Most of the students passed the test' and then wants to add the exact number. Which phrase fits best? '___, 87 out of 100.'
options: Let me put it another way
blocks.explain: **To be more precise** adds the exact detail: *most* becomes *87 out of 100*. *Let me put it another way* starts a whole new explanation, but she isn't changing her point. *What's it called?* is for a missing word, and nothing is missing here.

id.prompt: Dr. Wulan memaparkan hasil survei di Yogyakarta. Dia berkata 'Most of the students passed the test' lalu ingin menambahkan angka yang persis. Frasa mana yang paling cocok? '___, 87 out of 100.'
id.explain: **To be more precise** menambahkan detail yang persis: *most* menjadi *87 out of 100*. *Let me put it another way* memulai penjelasan yang sama sekali baru, padahal dia tidak mengubah poinnya. *What's it called?* untuk kata yang hilang, dan di sini tidak ada kata yang hilang.

id.title: Saat kata tidak kunjung muncul: parafrase dan perbaikan

material.title: Turning it up or down: intensifiers and softeners

blocks.text:
Recap from B2 collocations: some partners are fixed (*highly likely, deeply concerned, bitterly disappointed, fully aware*; *strongly agree*, but not *strongly unlikely*). From hedging you know *arguably* and *to some extent*. Now the finer controls.

**1. Words that are already 'maximum' take strong partners.** Most adjectives (*kata sifat*) can be graded (*bertingkat*): *tired, important, cold, good* → *a bit / quite / very / extremely tired*. Others already mean the top of the scale, so they **can't be graded** (*non-gradable*): *exhausted* (= extremely tired), *essential* (= absolutely necessary), *vital, freezing, furious, delighted, perfect, impossible, ridiculous*. With these, use **absolutely, utterly, completely, totally** (*really* also works), **not very**:
- ✓ *absolutely vital*, *utterly exhausted*, *completely impossible*
- ✗ *very vital*, ✗ *very freezing*, ✗ *slightly perfect*
Why? *very* means 'higher than usual on a scale', and these words are already at the top. **utterly** is mostly used with negative or unwelcome ideas (*utterly exhausted, utterly ridiculous, utterly unacceptable*); **absolutely** works with both (*absolutely delighted, absolutely right*).

**2. Softeners** (*downtoners*: kata yang melunakkan) turn a point down: *a little / a bit* (informal), *slightly* (a small amount), *somewhat* (agak; more formal), *rather* (see the tip below).

**3. Precise stance phrases:**
- **arguably** (bisa dibilang): an opinion you can defend: *arguably the best café in Bandung*.
- **to some extent** (sampai batas tertentu): partly true.
- **by no means** (sama sekali tidak): a strong *not*: *Success is by no means guaranteed.*
- **far from** + adjective or noun (jauh dari): *far from perfect, far from easy, far from over, far from ideal*. Polite in form, strong in meaning: *far from ideal* usually means 'quite bad'.

Indonesian traps: *jauh dari kata sempurna* → **far from perfect**, not *far from the word perfect*. And *sangat penting sekali* doubles the intensifier; in English one is enough.

id.text:
Ulasan dari kolokasi B2: beberapa pasangan kata sudah tetap (*highly likely, deeply concerned, bitterly disappointed, fully aware*; *strongly agree*, tapi bukan *strongly unlikely*). Dari hedging kamu tahu *arguably* dan *to some extent*. Sekarang kendali yang lebih halus.

**1. Kata yang sudah 'maksimal' butuh pasangan yang kuat.** Kebanyakan kata sifat bisa *bertingkat*: *tired, important, cold, good* → *a bit / quite / very / extremely tired*. Ada kata yang sudah bermakna puncak skala, jadi **tidak bisa bertingkat** (*non-gradable*): *exhausted* (= sangat lelah), *essential* (= mutlak perlu), *vital, freezing, furious, delighted, perfect, impossible, ridiculous*. Dengan kata-kata ini, pakai **absolutely, utterly, completely, totally** (*really* juga bisa), **bukan very**:
- ✓ *absolutely vital*, *utterly exhausted*, *completely impossible*
- ✗ *very vital*, ✗ *very freezing*, ✗ *slightly perfect*
Kenapa? *very* berarti 'lebih tinggi dari biasanya pada sebuah skala', sedangkan kata-kata ini sudah di puncak. **utterly** biasanya dipakai untuk hal negatif atau yang tidak diinginkan (*utterly exhausted, utterly ridiculous, utterly unacceptable*); **absolutely** bisa untuk keduanya (*absolutely delighted, absolutely right*).

**2. Pelunak** (*downtoners*: kata yang melunakkan) menurunkan kekuatan poin: *a little / a bit* (informal), *slightly* (sedikit), *somewhat* (agak; lebih formal), *rather* (lihat tip di bawah).

**3. Frasa sikap yang presisi:**
- **arguably** (bisa dibilang): pendapat yang bisa kamu pertahankan: *arguably the best café in Bandung*.
- **to some extent** (sampai batas tertentu): sebagian benar.
- **by no means** (sama sekali tidak): *tidak* yang kuat: *Success is by no means guaranteed.*
- **far from** + kata sifat atau kata benda (jauh dari): *far from perfect, far from easy, far from over, far from ideal*. Bentuknya sopan, maknanya kuat: *far from ideal* biasanya berarti 'cukup buruk'.

Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: *jauh dari kata sempurna* → **far from perfect**, bukan *far from the word perfect*. Dan *sangat penting sekali* memakai penguat dua kali; dalam bahasa Inggris satu saja cukup.

rows.en: After the night shift, the nurses were utterly exhausted.
rows.id: Setelah sif malam, para perawat benar-benar kelelahan.

rows.en: Good data is absolutely vital for this kind of research.
rows.id: Data yang bagus mutlak penting untuk penelitian seperti ini.

rows.id: Draf kedua agak lebih jelas daripada yang pertama.

rows.id: Keberhasilan sama sekali tidak terjamin.

blocks.text: **rather and quite: British vs American.** In British English, *rather* + a negative word softly criticises (*The hotel was rather expensive* = more than I wanted), but with a positive word it often shows a pleasant surprise and means *very*: *That talk was rather good!* (typical British understatement). **quite** + a gradable word means 'fairly' in British English (*quite good* = lumayan) but often 'very' in American English; with a non-gradable word it means 'completely' in both (*quite impossible, quite right*). In an international meeting, **slightly / somewhat** (to soften) and **very / extremely** (to strengthen) mean the same everywhere.

id.text: **rather dan quite: Britania vs Amerika.** Dalam bahasa Inggris Britania, *rather* + kata negatif mengkritik dengan halus (*The hotel was rather expensive* = lebih mahal dari yang saya mau), tapi dengan kata positif sering menunjukkan kejutan yang menyenangkan dan berarti *very*: *That talk was rather good!* (gaya merendah khas Inggris). **quite** + kata yang bertingkat berarti 'lumayan' dalam bahasa Inggris Britania (*quite good* = lumayan), tapi sering berarti 'sangat' dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika; dengan kata yang tidak bertingkat artinya 'sepenuhnya' di keduanya (*quite impossible, quite right*). Dalam rapat internasional, **slightly / somewhat** (untuk melunakkan) dan **very / extremely** (untuk menguatkan) artinya sama di mana-mana.

blocks.prompt: It's 3°C in the meeting room of a hotel in Dieng. Which sentence is natural?
blocks.explain: *freezing* already means 'extremely cold', the top of the scale, so it takes **absolutely** (or *really*). *very freezing* sounds wrong because *very* is for words that can be graded (*very cold*). *slightly freezing* contradicts itself.

id.prompt: Suhu di ruang rapat sebuah hotel di Dieng 3°C. Kalimat mana yang wajar?
id.explain: *freezing* sudah berarti 'sangat dingin', puncak skala, jadi pasangannya **absolutely** (atau *really*). *very freezing* terdengar salah karena *very* untuk kata yang bisa bertingkat (*very cold*). *slightly freezing* bertentangan dengan dirinya sendiri.

id.intro: Di C2, beda antara bahasa Inggris yang bagus dan yang istimewa sering hanya satu kata: concerned atau alarmed, annoyed atau furious, slightly atau dramatically. Di pelajaran ini kamu akan memilih kata dengan kekuatan yang pas, tetap bicara dengan mulus saat sebuah kata tiba-tiba hilang, dan menaikkan atau menurunkan kekuatan poinmu dengan pasangan kata yang tepat. Pemanasan: ingat-ingat kapan terakhir kali sebuah kata bahasa Inggris sudah di ujung lidah tapi tidak keluar. Apa yang kamu lakukan?
suggestedQuestions: Apakah boleh sesekali memakai kata bahasa Indonesia dalam rapat berbahasa Inggris?
Kenapa saya tidak boleh bilang 'very essential'?

assessment.rf-1: Bu Ani sedang menulis pernyataan yang tenang dan formal untuk dinas kesehatan kota Surabaya tentang sedikit kenaikan kasus demam berdarah. Dia tidak ingin membuat siapa pun takut. Pilih kata terbaik dari daftar ini: concerned, alarmed, panicked. 'We are ___ about the rise in dengue cases and are monitoring the situation closely.'
assessment.rf-2: Sebuah koran di Jakarta memberitakan bahwa seorang direktur perusahaan mungkin membayar suap untuk memenangkan kontrak pemerintah. Polisi sedang menyelidiki, dan belum ada yang terbukti di pengadilan. Pilih kata terbaik dari daftar ini: alleged, asserted, criticised. 'The director denies any involvement in the ___ bribe.'
assessment.rf-3: Dalam wawancara kerja di Jakarta, Dimas menjelaskan proyek terakhirnya, tapi pewawancara tampak bingung. Dimas ingin mulai lagi dan menjelaskannya dengan cara yang sama sekali berbeda. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: Let me put it another ___.
assessment.rf-4: Dalam rapat proyek di Bandung, Sari bilang pekerjaannya akan memakan waktu tiga minggu, lalu langsung meralatnya dengan perkiraan yang lebih akurat. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: It'll take three weeks, or ___ closer to four.
assessment.rf-5: Dalam panggilan video dengan mitra di Melbourne, Budi lupa kata 'stapler'. Daripada berhenti, dia menjelaskan fungsinya. Lengkapi dengan satu kata bahasa Inggris: It's the ___ you use to join sheets of paper together with a small piece of metal.
assessment.rf-6: Di sebuah kafe di Bandung, harga kopi sekarang Rp 2.000 lebih mahal daripada bulan lalu, dan pelanggan tidak mengeluh. Pemiliknya ingin membuat perubahan itu terdengar kecil, tapi jujur. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: The new prices are ___ higher than last month's.
assessment.rf-7: Timmu pindah ke kantor baru di Yogyakarta. Kantornya tidak punya jendela, liftnya rusak dan Wi-Fi-nya terus putus. Dalam email ke manajermu, kamu ingin mengatakan dengan sopan tapi jelas bahwa kantor itu sama sekali tidak bagus. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: The new office is ___ from ideal.
